propositions.text: This is an appeal and cross-appeal from a Federal Court designated judge's decision on disclosure of redacted warrant and affidavit content under Canada Evidence Act.
propositions.quote: This is an appeal and cross-appeal from a decision (Public Reasons) of a designated judge of the Federal Court (the Designated Judge) seized with an application pursuant to paragraph 38.04(2)(c) of the Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5 (the CEA) to disclose the redacted content of a warrant issued by the Federal Court in 2013 (the Warrant) and the affidavit filed in support thereof (the Affidavit).

propositions.text: The Designated Judge ordered disclosure of some information under subsection 38.06(2) and other information not subject to section 38 of the CEA.
propositions.quote: The Designated Judge ordered the disclosure of some of the information pursuant to subsection 38.06(2), and of other information not properly the subject of section 38 of the CEA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this appeal and cross-appeal concern a Federal Court judge's order to disclose some redacted warrant and affidavit information under the Canada Evidence Act.

propositions.text: The Attorney General contends the Designated Judge erred in fact and law by ordering disclosure, breached natural justice, and exceeded jurisdiction regarding non-CEA information.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General of Canada (the Attorney General or the appellant) contends that the Designated Judge erred in fact and law by ordering the disclosure of such information, erred in law by ordering disclosure of some information contrary to the requirements of natural justice and procedural fairness, and exceeded his jurisdiction with respect to the information that was not the subject of section 38 of the CEA.

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General argues the judge erred in ordering disclosure, breached natural justice, and exceeded jurisdiction on some information.

propositions.text: Mr. Huang argues the Designated Judge erred by refusing to disclose some redacted information and mischaracterizing the amicus curiae's role.
propositions.quote: On cross-appeal, Qing (Quentin) Huang (Mr. Huang or the respondent) argues that the Designated Judge erred by refusing to order the disclosure of some redacted information, and in determining the role of the amicus curiae in this case.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Huang argues the judge erred by refusing some disclosure and mischaracterizing the amicus curiae's role.

propositions.text: The appeal hearing occurred in two phases: a public hearing on March 6, 2018, and an in camera ex parte hearing on March 7-8, 2018.
propositions.quote: The hearing of this appeal took place in two phases. In a public hearing held on March 6, 2018, the Court heard the arguments of the appellant and respondent on cross-appeal, essentially revolving around the test for relevance applied by the Designated Judge in his assessment of the section 38 application, and his interpretation of the amicus’ role. In an in camera ex parte hearing that took place on March 7 and 8, 2018, the Attorney General and the amicus dealt mostly with the arguments raised on appeal by the Attorney General.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the two-phase hearing: public on March 6 and in camera ex parte on March 7-8, 2018.

propositions.text: These public reasons address the cross-appeal; private reasons addressing other issues were released concurrently and kept confidential.
propositions.quote: These public reasons deal with the cross-appeal. A set of private reasons, released concurrently with these public reasons, has been made available to the Attorney General and the amicus only, and is kept at the designated proceedings facility in Ottawa, Ontario. The private reasons address the issues that were debated in the private hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court states these public reasons address the cross-appeal; private reasons address other issues confidentially.

propositions.text: Mr. Huang was arrested Nov 30, 2013, charged with conspiracy to provide military secrets to China under Security of Information Act.
propositions.quote: Mr. Huang was arrested and charged on November 30, 2013 with conspiracy to provide Canadian military secrets to the government of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), contrary to the Security of Information Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. O-5.

propositions.text: Key evidence was intercepted calls to PRC Embassy by CSIS under a 2013 Federal Court warrant issued under CSIS Act section 21.
propositions.quote: A key piece of evidence that led to Mr. Huang’s arrest were telephone calls that he allegedly made to the PRC Embassy in Ottawa, incidentally intercepted by the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) pursuant to the Warrant issued by the Federal Court on March 7, 2013 under section 21 of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-23 (the CSIS Act).

propositions.text: The warrant authorized interception of calls to/from a CSIS target at PRC Embassy; Mr. Huang was not a target or under CSIS investigation.
propositions.quote: Among other matters, it authorized the interception of telephone calls to and from a CSIS target at the PRC Embassy in Ottawa. The intercepted conversation between Mr. Huang and the PRC Embassy took place on May 22, 2013. Mr. Huang was not a target of the Warrant and had never been under investigation by CSIS.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Mr. Huang's arrest for conspiracy, evidence from intercepted calls under a CSIS warrant, and that he was not a CSIS target.

propositions.text: CSIS gave intercepted call transcripts to RCMP under CSIS Act section 19 for investigation or prosecution.
propositions.quote: The transcripts and recordings of the intercepted calls allegedly made by Mr. Huang to the Embassy of the PRC were provided by CSIS to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (the RCMP) under the authority of section 19 of the CSIS Act, which provides that such information may be disclosed to a peace officer if it may be used in the investigation or prosecution of an alleged contravention of any law of Canada or a province.

propositions.text: The PPSC disclosed redacted warrant and affidavit to Mr. Huang but refused unredacted versions citing section 38 CEA protections.
propositions.quote: These transcripts were disclosed to Mr. Huang by the Public Prosecution Service of Canada (the PPSC), as part of its disclosure obligations pursuant to R. v. Stinchcombe... A heavily redacted version of the Warrant and the Affidavit were also disclosed to the respondent. The PPSC declined to provide the unredacted content of the two documents to the respondent and his counsel, on the grounds that to do so would result in the disclosure of sensitive information or potentially injurious information as defined in section 38 of the CEA.

propositions.text: No notice was given to Attorney General under subsection 38.01(1) because PPSC believed respondent would not challenge admissibility or seek disclosure.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, no notice was given to the Attorney General pursuant to subsection 38.01(1), because counsel for the PPSC believed the respondent did not intend to challenge the admissibility of the intercepted communications and that there was no possibility of disclosure of the redacted information.

paragraphs.summary: The court states CSIS gave transcripts to RCMP; PPSC disclosed redacted warrant and affidavit but refused unredacted versions citing section 38; no notice to Attorney General.

propositions.text: Respondent changed counsel in 2016, who requested more info and considered application to exclude intercepted calls under Charter section 8 and 24(2).
propositions.quote: The respondent, however, changed counsel in the fall of 2016. His new counsel requested additional information from the PPSC regarding the Warrant and advised the PPSC that they were considering bringing an application before the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to seek the exclusion of the intercepted telephone communications pursuant to the principles laid out in R. v. Garofoli...

propositions.text: The application challenges warrant validity and lawfulness of interceptions, seeking exclusion of evidence as more intrusive than necessary.
propositions.quote: That application is “for an order that the 2013 warrant was invalid, the interceptions were not authorized by law and infringed section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms”... and that therefore the evidence obtained should be excluded pursuant to subsection 24(2) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms... In support of such an application, Mr. Huang is seeking to show that the search authorized by the Warrant was more intrusive than was reasonably necessary to achieve its objectives...

paragraphs.summary: The court explains respondent changed counsel, who sought more info and planned application to exclude intercepted calls as unlawful and overly intrusive.

propositions.text: PPSC informed Attorney General of possible disclosure on Feb 27, 2017; respondent applied to Federal Court same day for disclosure.
propositions.quote: The PPSC therefore informed the Attorney General of the possible disclosure of the redacted information in the Warrant and Affidavit on February 27, 2017. Mr. Huang brought an application for disclosure before the Federal Court on that same date.

propositions.text: Respondent claims he cannot challenge interception lawfulness without redacted information withheld from him.
propositions.quote: In his Notice of Application, the respondent claimed that he cannot investigate or challenge the lawfulness of the interception of private communications that form the basis for his criminal charges without the redacted information that is being withheld from him.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge's decision on this application is now before this Court on appeal.
propositions.quote: It is the Designated Judge’s decision on this application that is before this Court in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states PPSC informed Attorney General of disclosure possibility; respondent applied for disclosure claiming need to challenge interception; judge's decision is appealed.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge summarized background, legal context, and principles governing the disclosure proceeding; no need to repeat here.
propositions.quote: After having provided the background relevant to this case and summarized in broad detail the public affidavit in support of the appellant’s position that the disclosure of the redacted information would be injurious to national security, the Designated Judge set out the CSIS Act warrant regime and the legislative scheme pursuant to which the Attorney General’s decision to authorize disclosure is reviewed. There is no need to repeat here the Designated Judge’s well-crafted summary of the legal context and principles governing this proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Designated Judge summarized background and legal principles governing disclosure; no repetition needed here.

propositions.text: CSIS mandate is to prevent threats to Canada's security by collecting information and advising government, unlike police investigations.
propositions.quote: Suffice it to emphasize that contrary to police investigations, which are focused on particular crimes committed by identifiable individuals, the mandate of CSIS is to prevent activities that would put the security of Canada at risk. In that context, CSIS’ task is to collect information that may assist in that mission and report to and advise the Government of Canada (see s. 12 of the CSIS Act).

propositions.text: Section 21 CSIS Act allows Federal Court judge to issue warrant only if facts justify belief on reasonable grounds of threat to security, presence of threat, and failure of other measures.
propositions.quote: While the notion of “threats to the security of Canada” is broadly defined in section 2 of the CSIS Act, the requirements to obtain from the Federal Court a warrant to collect information and intelligence are strict. Section 21 of the CSIS Act provides that a judge may issue a warrant authorizing the interception of communications and the search and seizure of information only if he or she is satisfied that the facts affirmed in the affidavit in support of the application for a warrant justify the belief, on reasonable grounds, that: (1) a warrant is required to investigate a threat to the security of Canada; (2) the threat as defined by section 2 of the CSIS Act is present; and (3) other investigative measures have been tried and have either failed or are unlikely to succeed.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains CSIS's mandate to prevent security threats and the strict warrant requirements under section 21 of the CSIS Act.

propositions.text: Historically, courts could not second-guess Crown's public interest privilege claims on national security documents.
propositions.quote: There was a time when courts were precluded from second-guessing the assertion by the Crown of a public interest privilege, and could not inspect documents allegedly pertaining to international relations, national security or defence.

propositions.text: Common law and subsection 41(2) Federal Court Act entrenched this privilege (Duncan v. Cammell Laird & Co.; Landreville v. The Queen).
propositions.quote: That doctrine was firmly entrenched in common law (see Duncan v. Cammell Laird & Co., [1942] A.C. 624, [1942] 1 All E.R. 587) and was enshrined in subsection 41(2) of the Federal Court Act, R.S.C. 1970 (2nd Supp.), c. 10 (see Landreville v. The Queen (1976), 70 D.L.R. (3d) 122, [1977] 1 F.C. 419).

propositions.text: Following 1981 Commission recommendation, section 41 Federal Court Act was repealed and replaced by sections 38 and 38.01-38.15 of the CEA.
propositions.quote: Following the recommendation of the Commission of Inquiry Concerning Certain Activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Second Report - Vol. 1: Freedom and Security under the Law, Ottawa, August 1981, section 41 of the Federal Court Act was repealed and replaced by what are now sections 38 and 38.01 to 38.15 of the CEA.

propositions.text: Now designated Federal Court judges determine whether protected government information should be disclosed under the CEA.
propositions.quote: It is now for designated judges of the Federal Court to determine whether, and under what conditions, the information that the government seeks to protect ought to be disclosed.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains historical public interest privilege and its replacement by CEA provisions empowering Federal Court judges to decide disclosure.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge summarized principles from Federal Court and FCA applying CEA provisions, including Ribic test for lifting disclosure prohibition.
propositions.quote: The Designated Judge aptly summarized the principles that have been developed over the years by the Federal Court and this Court in applying those provisions of the CEA. Of particular relevance is the test established by this Court in Ribic v. Canada (Attorney General)...

propositions.text: The Ribic test requires: (1) judge decides if info is relevant; (2) if relevant, if disclosure would injure national interests; (3) if injury shown, balance public interest in disclosure vs non-disclosure.
propositions.quote: For the purpose of this appeal, I need only reproduce his synopsis of the three part test when assessing the merits of the section 38 privilege claims: First, the judge must decide whether the information sought to be protected is relevant to the underlying proceeding. Where the judge finds that the information is relevant, the next step is to determine whether disclosure would be injurious to international relations, national defence or national security, as outlined in section 38.06 of the CEA. Where the Attorney General can show a reasonable basis for her assessment that the disclosure of the information at issue would cause injury to the national interests, the judge must then determine whether the public interest in disclosure is outweighed by the public interest in non-disclosure.

propositions.text: The court endorses the Designated Judge's summary of the Ribic test for section 38 privilege claims.
propositions.quote: Again, the Designated Judge appropriately explained that test in paragraphs 44 to 52 of his Public Reasons, and I can do no better than to endorse his summary of the case law in that respect.

paragraphs.summary: The court endorses the Designated Judge's summary of the Ribic test for disclosure under section 38 of the CEA.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge found redacted info unrelated to interception not relevant to challenge warrant authorization under World Bank Group v. Wallace test.
propositions.quote: Acknowledging that the Court must be sensitive to the value that the redacted information could have to the respondent’s right to make full answer and defence, the Designated Judge nevertheless found that the redacted information unrelated to the interception of Mr. Huang’s telephone calls would not be relevant to challenge the authorization of the Warrant. In his view, the redacted information would not be relevant to either of the grounds identified by the Supreme Court in World Bank Group v. Wallace...

paragraphs.summary: The Designated Judge found unrelated redacted information not relevant to challenge the warrant under Wallace test.

propositions.text: The Attorney General satisfied burden that disclosure of much redacted info would injure national security and international relations.
propositions.quote: The Designated Judge also found that the Attorney General had satisfied her burden of establishing that disclosure of much of the redacted information would cause injury to Canada’s national security and international relations.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge accepted the mosaic theory that discrete innocuous info can harm security when combined.
propositions.quote: In coming to that conclusion, the Designated Judge noted and accepted what has come to be known as the mosaic theory, according to which discrete pieces of information that appear to be innocuous when considered separately may well be harmful to Canada’s security interests when put together.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge acknowledged foreign agency info may limit disclosure to affected individuals.
propositions.quote: The Designated Judge also acknowledged that information provided by foreign agencies may well limit the disclosure of information to affected individuals.

paragraphs.summary: The Designated Judge found Attorney General met burden showing disclosure would harm national security, accepted mosaic theory, and noted foreign agency limits.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge reviewed each disputed redaction, applied Ribic test, and found most info either irrelevant or disclosure risk outweighed public interest.
propositions.quote: In his conclusion, the Designated Judge explained that he read the underlying text of each disputed redaction subject to a CEA section 38 privilege claim, and made a determination on whether the information could be disclosed applying the Ribic test in a chart attached as a schedule to a private judgment issued concurrently with his Public Reasons. He found that much of the information sought by the respondent “is either not relevant or that the risk of injury has been established by the Attorney General and that the public interest in non-disclosure outweighs that of disclosure” (at para. 80).

propositions.text: He also considered exercising discretion under subsection 38.06(2) to authorize partial or full disclosure of relevant info.
propositions.quote: He also considered whether to exercise his discretion pursuant to subsection 38.06(2) of the CEA to authorize the disclosure in whole or in part of relevant information.

paragraphs.summary: The Designated Judge applied Ribic test to each redaction, found most info irrelevant or disclosure risk outweighed interest, and considered discretion to disclose.

propositions.text: Cross-appeal raises two issues: correct relevance threshold in Ribic test for section 38 disclosure, and whether Designated Judge erred on amicus role.
propositions.quote: As previously mentioned, these public reasons deal only with the respondent’s cross-appeal. In his cross-appeal, Mr. Huang essentially raises two issues: What is the correct threshold for relevance within the Ribic test in an application for disclosure pursuant to section 38 of the CEA? Did the Designated Judge err in determining the role of the amicus in the present proceeding? IV. Analysis A. What is the correct threshold for relevance within the Ribic test in an application for disclosure pursuant to section 38 of the CEA?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies cross-appeal issues: correct relevance threshold in Ribic test and Designated Judge's amicus role determination.

propositions.text: Respondent argues Designated Judge erred by requiring proof of 'reasonable likelihood' of relevance and ignoring 'manner of search' argument.
propositions.quote: The respondent submits that the Designated Judge made two errors in assessing the relevance of the redacted information, first by wrongly requiring him to prove a “reasonable likelihood” of relevance, and second by failing to consider the possibility of a “manner of search” argument on his challenge to the admissibility of the intercepted telephone calls.

propositions.text: Court finds neither argument warranted when reading Designated Judge's Public Reasons contextually.
propositions.quote: In my view, neither of these arguments is warranted when the Designated Judge’s Public Reasons are read contextually.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues judge erred on relevance threshold and manner of search; court rejects these arguments on contextual reading.

propositions.text: Unclear if CSIS shared unredacted or redacted warrant and affidavit with RCMP; if redacted, O’Connor rule for third party production may apply.
propositions.quote: It is not entirely clear from the record whether CSIS shared with the RCMP the unredacted Warrant and Affidavit on the basis of which the calls by Mr. Huang to the PRC Embassy were intercepted, or only the redacted version that was disclosed by the Crown as part of its Stinchcombe obligations. If it is the latter, the O’Connor rule pursuant to which an accused must show a “reasonable likelihood” that the records will be of probative value to obtain third party production in the Garofoli context would probably apply...

propositions.text: O’Connor rule requires accused to show reasonable likelihood of probative value to obtain third party production in Garofoli context.
propositions.quote: If it is the latter, the O’Connor rule pursuant to which an accused must show a “reasonable likelihood” that the records will be of probative value to obtain third party production in the Garofoli context would probably apply...

propositions.text: CSIS is generally a third party for disclosure when investigations are separate (citing Ahmad, Nuttall, Jaser, Alizadeh).
propositions.quote: This would be the case because it is generally accepted that, where CSIS and the RCMP investigations are separate, CSIS is a third party for disclosure purposes (see R. v. Ahmad...; R. v. Nuttall...; R. v. Jaser...; R. v. Alizadeh...).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes uncertainty if CSIS shared unredacted or redacted warrant; if redacted, O’Connor rule for third party production likely applies; CSIS is a third party.

propositions.text: Court finds Designated Judge did not apply 'reasonable likelihood' standard from third party disclosure context but proper legal test for relevance in Ribic analysis.
propositions.quote: Be that as it may, I do not think the Judge applied a “reasonable likelihood” of relevance standard developed in the context of third party disclosure, as alleged by the respondent. When read as a whole, the Public Reasons clearly demonstrate that the Judge applied the proper legal test to establish relevance at the first stage of his Ribic analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Designated Judge applied the proper legal test for relevance, not the 'reasonable likelihood' standard from third party disclosure.

propositions.text: The Crown fulfilled its disclosure obligation according to the Stinchcombe standard as conceded by PPSC counsel.
propositions.quote: he identified the standard according to which the Crown fulfilled its disclosure obligation as that established by the Supreme Court in Stinchcombe

propositions.text: For this appeal, the Warrant and Affidavit contents are assumed to be first party disclosure.
propositions.quote: it is to be assumed, for the purposes of this appeal, that the contents of the Warrant and of the Affidavit are first party disclosure

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Crown met disclosure obligations per Stinchcombe and assumes Warrant and Affidavit are first party disclosure for this appeal.

propositions.text: The Judge noted a Supplementary Notice seeking further disclosure about PRC Embassy call interceptions was outside his application scope.
propositions.quote: The Judge found that the subject matter of this further application was outside the scope of the application that was before him

propositions.text: The information sought, if it exists, is held by third party CSIS and a production application is set for Ontario Superior Court under O’Connor.
propositions.quote: the information in question, if it exists, was in the possession of a third party (CSIS), and that an application for the production of that information was set down to be heard in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice pursuant to O’Connor

propositions.text: The Judge was aware of the distinction between relevance standards for Crown-held versus third party documents.
propositions.quote: This is clear evidence that the Judge was well aware of the distinction between the two standards for relevance, depending upon whether the documents sought by an accused are in the hands of the Crown or of a third party

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Judge recognized the further disclosure application was outside scope and understood relevance standards differ for Crown versus third party documents.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge summarized the law and Ribic test for section 38 CEA, emphasizing a low relevance threshold.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge summarized the applicable law and, in particular, the test developed in Ribic for the purposes of section 38 of the CEA

propositions.text: The relevance threshold is low, especially to protect the accused's right to full answer and defence.
propositions.quote: the Court “must be particularly conscious of the value, if any, of the redacted information to the Applicant’s right to make full answer and defence to the charges against him”

propositions.text: If information is not reasonably useful to the defence, it is not relevant and no further assessment is needed.
propositions.quote: If the information at issue may not be reasonably useful to the defence, it is not relevant and there is no need to go any further in assessing it

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Judge applied Ribic's low relevance threshold, requiring information to be reasonably useful to the defence to be relevant.

propositions.text: Ribic requires judges to determine if information is relevant in the Stinchcombe sense, meaning reasonably useful to the defence.
propositions.quote: The first task of a judge hearing an application is to determine whether the information sought to be disclosed is relevant or not in the usual and common sense of the Stinchcombe rule

propositions.text: This relevance threshold is low and requires inspection of information; onus is on party seeking disclosure to show likely relevance.
propositions.quote: This is undoubtedly a low threshold... The onus is on the party seeking disclosure to establish that the information is in all likelihood relevant evidence

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Ribic explaining the low relevance threshold and onus on the party seeking disclosure to show likely relevance.

propositions.text: The Designated Judge applied the Stinchcombe test correctly, recognizing relevance as usefulness to the defence.
propositions.quote: he reiterated... that the information... would not be reasonably useful to the defence in the underlying criminal proceeding, “in the Stinchcombe sense of relevance”

propositions.text: The Judge did not confuse the Stinchcombe test with the Garofoli test for third party production.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge did not confuse the two tests and properly applied the Stinchcombe test in his assessment of relevance

propositions.text: It was unfortunate for the Judge to comment on the Garofoli stage, but it did not affect his correct application of the Stinchcombe test.
propositions.quote: It may have been unfortunate for the Designated Judge to comment on what will happen at the Garofoli stage... but he was clearly alert to the distinction

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Judge correctly applied the Stinchcombe test and did not confuse it with the Garofoli test despite some comments.

propositions.text: The Judge erred by assuming the constitutional challenge rested only on two bases, ignoring manner of intercept challenge.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge erred in assuming that his challenge... rests only on two possible bases... failed to consider... manner by which the intercepts were carried out

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Judge erred by ignoring a manner of intercept constitutional challenge.

propositions.text: The Judge referred to facial and sub-facial validity arguments and Supreme Court discussion in Wallace.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge did refer at paragraph 60... to the facial and sub-facial validity arguments and mentioned that, in Wallace, the Supreme Court discussed these two grounds

propositions.text: One cannot infer the Judge was unaware of the manner of search challenge possibility from that statement.
propositions.quote: I do not think... that one can infer... that the Designated Judge was oblivious to the possibility of a manner of search challenge

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Judge acknowledged validity arguments and was not oblivious to manner of search challenge possibility.

propositions.text: A search may be unreasonable if the authorization is too broad or minimization principles are not followed.
propositions.quote: a search... may be unreasonable... if... the issuing justice failed to limit the breadth... or... persons carrying out the search failed to adhere to minimization principles

propositions.text: The Judge was aware of manner of search issues and cited case law on minimization and reasonable intrusiveness.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge was well aware of that possibility and alluded to it at paragraph 13... he cited the same case law relied upon by the respondent

propositions.text: The Judge refused to entertain a further notice of application on manner of execution as premature but was alert to the challenge possibility.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge refused to entertain that further notice of application because it was premature... but he was clearly alert to the fact that the respondent was considering the possibility

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Judge knew of manner of search issues, cited relevant law, and was alert to the respondent's challenge possibility.

propositions.text: It cannot be seriously argued the Judge erred in appreciating the manner of search argument.
propositions.quote: I do not think it can seriously be argued that the Designated Judge erred in failing to appreciate the manner of search argument

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Judge did not err in appreciating the manner of search argument.

propositions.text: The Judge made no legal error concluding redacted Warrant and Affidavit info on interceptions is not reasonably useful to defence.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge made no error of law when he concluded that the redacted information... would not be reasonably useful or relevant to his defence

propositions.text: Warrant and Affidavit pre-date interceptions and cannot show how communications were intercepted or privacy impacts.
propositions.quote: the Warrant and the Affidavit necessarily pre-date the interceptions themselves; none of the information... can be of relevance with respect to how the communications were actually intercepted

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Judge correctly concluded redacted Warrant and Affidavit info is not useful to defence regarding interception manner.

propositions.text: The respondent can argue the search was unreasonable due to Warrant's failure to limit authorization breadth.
propositions.quote: he is entitled to argue... that the search was not carried out in a reasonable manner because the Warrant failed to limit the breadth of the authorization

propositions.text: The respondent is not entitled to question minimization sufficiency for every search type authorized by the Warrant.
propositions.quote: he is not entitled to question the sufficiency of the minimization measures in relation to every type of search and seizure authorized by the Warrant

propositions.text: The Warrant is severable; focus is on interception of calls to/from PRC Embassy.
propositions.quote: The Warrant is severable... The focus of the enquiry, therefore, is on the interception of telephone calls to and from the PRC Embassy

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent may argue unreasonable search breadth but not minimization for all searches; focus is on PRC Embassy call interceptions.

propositions.text: The Warrant contains clauses on retention and use of intercepted communications disclosed to respondent.
propositions.quote: The Warrant contains a number of clauses, dealing with the conditions associated with the retention of intercepted communications and the use to which they can be put

propositions.text: Respondent can rely on disclosed clauses to argue insufficiency against section 8 Charter privacy rights.
propositions.quote: he is certainly entitled to rely on them in trying to convince the Garofoli judge that they are insufficient to guard against unreasonable intrusions on privacy rights pursuant to section 8 of the Charter

propositions.text: Other undisclosed Warrant clauses impose minimization conditions limiting authorization breadth for national security reasons.
propositions.quote: other clauses... impose minimization conditions that limit the breadth of the authorization

paragraphs.summary: The court notes disclosed Warrant clauses can be relied on by respondent, while undisclosed clauses impose minimization limits for security.

propositions.text: On Garofoli application, respondent can rely on Affidavit to show minimization insufficiency.
propositions.quote: the respondent would also undoubtedly be entitled to rely on the Affidavit in support of the Warrant to show that the minimization measures are insufficient

propositions.text: CSIS warrants differ from criminal warrants; statutory requirements and scope differ due to different purposes.
propositions.quote: a CSIS warrant is substantially different from a criminal warrant... they are directed at different purposes

propositions.text: Affidavit for CSIS warrant is broader and much may be irrelevant to a particular criminal investigation.
propositions.quote: the information found in an affidavit supporting a CSIS warrant is much broader in scope, and significant portions of it may not be relevant in the context of a particular criminal investigation

propositions.text: Respondent's reliance on R. v. Thompson is of limited assistance due to these differences.
propositions.quote: the respondent’s reliance on R. v. Thompson... is of limited assistance

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent can rely on Affidavit for minimization issues but CSIS warrants differ from criminal ones, limiting Thompson's relevance.

propositions.text: The Judge correctly applied the low relevance threshold in Ribic and excluded unrelated redacted information as irrelevant.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge did not err in his analysis of the relevance test... He correctly assessed the relevance threshold to be low, yet properly concluded that redacted information unrelated to Mr. Huang’s intercepted calls would not be relevant

propositions.text: Limited redacted info related to Embassy calls could have been more useful to appellant but was renounced for national security.
propositions.quote: the limited redacted information related to the interception of telephone calls to and from the Embassy could have been more useful to the appellant than to the respondent. Still, the appellant renounced that potential benefit for national security reasons

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Judge correctly applied Ribic's relevance test and that redacted info unrelated to calls was irrelevant; appellant renounced some info for security.

propositions.text: Respondent objects to Judge's comment limiting amicus role, arguing it should be like defence counsel or special advocate.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the respondent takes exception with a comment... that amicus curiae can “play only a limited role”... should be more akin to the role played by a defence counsel or a special advocate

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Judge erred by limiting the amicus role, which should be like defence counsel or special advocate.

propositions.text: Section 38 CEA does not explicitly provide for amicus; appointment and role are judicial discretion.
propositions.quote: section 38 of the CEA does not explicitly provide for the possibility to appoint an amicus. It is as a matter of judicial discretion that... the practice to appoint an amicus

propositions.text: Amicus is not accused's lawyer or special advocate; role is to assist court and serve court's interests.
propositions.quote: the amicus is not the accused’s lawyer... The role of the amicus is to assist the court and ensure the proper administration of justice, and the sole “client” of the amicus is the court

propositions.text: Amicus must act transparently and not act as advocate for accused or respondent, but provide court insight.
propositions.quote: He or she must therefore act at all times with transparency, without ever attempting to take counsel for the Attorney General by surprise

paragraphs.summary: The court explains amicus role is judicially appointed to assist the court, not act as defence counsel or special advocate, and must act transparently.

propositions.text: The Judge directed amicus to assist under section 38 CEA to balance disclosure and national security.
propositions.quote: the Designated Judge directed Mr. Kapoor, in his role as amicus, to “assist the Court in performing its statutory obligations under section 38 of the CEA”

propositions.text: Amicus fulfilled role admirably and was helpful to both the Designated Judge and this Court in the appeal.
propositions.quote: the amicus fulfilled his role admirably, professionally and with an acute understanding of his function... was equally helpful to this Court in this appeal

propositions.text: The interests of justice were well served by amicus's active participation throughout proceedings.
propositions.quote: there is no doubt in my mind that the interests of justice were well served by his active participation throughout these proceedings

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the amicus fulfilled his role professionally and served the interests of justice well in these proceedings.

propositions.text: The cross-appeal is dismissed; the appeal is allowed in part and remitted to the Designated Judge for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the cross-appeal... I would allow the appeal in part and remit the matter back to the Designated Judge for reconsideration

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the cross-appeal, allows the appeal in part, and remits the matter to the Designated Judge for reconsideration.
